summary: Proposes an optional template for IETF patent disclosures and licensing declarations. It is meant to simplify the process and help disclosers provide the information required of them.

eli5.summary: A fill-in-the-blanks form for people to tell the group about any patents that might matter.

questions: how to disclose a patent to the ietf
how do i disclose a patent to the ietf
what are the ietf patent licensing options
what is a necessary patent claim
subtitle: A standard form for disclosing patents that affect IETF standards.

tldr.problem: IETF participants must disclose patents that might be essential to standards being developed, and patent holders must declare how they will license those patents. The process was confusing because no standard form existed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides a single-page template that asks for patent information, identifies which IETF documents the patent affects, and offers five licensing options: no license required, royalty-free licensing, reasonable licensing (with possible fees), defer decision, or unwilling to commit.
tldr.outcome: The optional template simplifies compliance with IETF patent disclosure rules and helps patent holders and IETF participants understand each other's intentions.

today: RFC 3905 remains an Informational reference for the IETF patent disclosure process. It has not been obsoleted, and the template is still recommended for use by IETF participants disclosing patents.

sections.title: Patent Disclosures and IETF Standards
sections.content:
The IETF develops open standards, but sometimes the standards depend on inventions covered by patents. RFC 3668 requires IETF participants to disclose patents they believe are essential to a standard being developed, and patent holders must state how they will license those patents to implementers. These obligations exist to ensure that standards are not locked behind undisclosed patents and that implementers understand the licensing terms they must accept.

RFC 3905 proposes an optional template to simplify this process. The template is not mandatory, but using it helps both disclosers meet their obligations and the IETF understand patent situations clearly.
sections.eli5: The IETF makes rules for the Internet. Sometimes a rule uses an idea someone patented. When that happens, the patent owner must tell the IETF what they will charge for a license, or if the license is free.

sections.title: The Template Structure
sections.content:
The template consists of eight sections. Sections I and II ask for the patent holder's legal name and contact information for license applications. Section III (optional) identifies the IETF participant whose belief that a patent is essential triggered the disclosure. Section IV specifies which IETF document the disclosure relates to: an RFC, Internet-Draft, or other contribution, plus identifying information.

Section V requests patent information. For granted patents or published applications, it asks for serial numbers, application dates, and countries. For unpublished pending applications, only a yes-no answer is required. The discloser may optionally identify which sections of the IETF document are alleged to be covered.

Section VI contains the licensing declaration. Section VII asks for submitter contact information. Section VIII provides space for additional notes or conditions on the disclosure.
sections.eli5: The form asks: Who are you? What patent? Which standard? Do you charge for a license or not? The form is designed to fit one page.

sections.title: The Five Licensing Options
sections.content:
A patent holder must select exactly one of five licensing options in Section VI of the template.

Option (a): No License Required. The patent holder waives the right to require a license. Implementers can use the standard without permission from the patent holder. An optional checkbox limits this commitment to standards-track RFCs only.

Option (b): Royalty-Free, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory. The patent holder will grant a free license to all implementers under reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. Again, a checkbox can limit this to standards-track RFCs.

Option (c): Reasonable and Non-Discriminatory, with Possible Royalty. The patent holder will license to all implementers on reasonable, non-discriminatory terms, but may charge a fee. The optional checkbox limits this to standards-track RFCs.

Option (d): Licensing Declaration to be Provided Later. The patent holder commits to one of options (a), (b), or (c) but defers specifying which one until a later date.

Option (e): Unwilling to Commit. The patent holder will not commit to any of the above options. This signals that the patent may pose a risk to implementers.
sections.eli5: Choose one: free, royalty-free, maybe charge, decide later, or we won't help. Most standards prefer free or royalty-free.

sections.title: Using the Template
sections.content:
The template is optional. IETF participants can use other formats or methods to disclose patents and declare licenses, provided they comply with RFC 3668. However, using the template makes compliance clear and simple.

A separate template must be submitted for each IETF document or contribution to which a patent disclosure relates. Patent holders should submit disclosures in English, the IETF's working language, and should present names and companies in English-language conventions.

Patent holders may use Section VIII (Other Notes) to clarify conditions or restrictions not fully captured by the standard options. For example, a patent holder might use this space to impose reciprocity requirements, or to declare that the license applies only to implementations of RFCs, not to Internet-Drafts.

Submitting the template does not grant an actual license; it only declares the patent holder's intention. The actual license agreement would come later, when an implementer requests one.
sections.eli5: Fill out the form for each patent and each standard. Use the notes section to explain anything special about your offer. Signing the form does not mean you gave anyone a license yet; it just promises what you would do.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Intellectual Property Rights in IETF Technology", BCP 79, RFC 3668, February 2004.
